Q: Why is Math.random being outperformed by crypto.getRandomValues? A:

The answer to "why is Math.random being outperformed by crypto.getRandomValues" was: Because Math.random was unnecessarily slow, and crypto.getRandomValues is very fast on Windows. At some point between April 2025 and January 2026, V8 has had a change that makes Math.random fast enough that it is now about to beat an entropy pool filled by crypto.getRandomValues, even on Windows.

Aside: There was a lot of gaslighting in this SO question by people who expected me to simply appeal to authority. Individuals made incorrect claims about "microbenchmarking" being inaccurate (that wasn't actually the case, jsbench.me tests did not suffer from dead code elimination, that was just a lazy assumption.) They then ignored further benchmarking, attempting to write off a benchmark that actually renders entropy to the screen as just another "microbenchmark," as if FPS are a social construct. They then went on to "correct" my benchmark, introducing a horrible NaN bug that killed the performance, making it appear as though their argument was correct when it wasn't. Another individual was very "helpful" by pointing out that It Works On My Machine™, as if Linux's /dev/urandom being incredibly slow somehow invalidates the results I got in Windows.

Q: maximum number of files/directories handled by dirent struct A:

readdir() allocates memory for every struct dirent it returns a pointer to. The dirents are deallocated automatically on closedir(), so you can't free() that memory when you no longer need any particular dirent, and you can't use any dirent after closedir(). I suppose it's possible (though not likely) that your program can't allocate more memory for dirents.
You could check errno after readdir() returns NULL to find out.

If that is the problem, you can instead use readdir_r(), which uses a dirent* to an allocation you provide (which could even be a local variable on the stack), and you could reuse it for all dirents, one after the other. One caveat with readdir_r() is that the size of struct dirent depends on the file system, and you need to ensure your allocation is big enough.

Q: GIT submodule active state is not working properly A:

I've never switched off submodules so I can only answer from documentation. AFAIU submodule.<name>.active and submodule.active are configuration values from .git/config, not from .gitmodules. submodule.<name>.active is a boolean that turns on/off the named submodule. submodule.active is a list of paths to active submodules. I.e. you can either do

git config submodule.my_doc_module.active false

to turn one submodule off or

git config --add submodule.active path1/to/module1
git config --add submodule.active path2/to/module2

to list only active submodules. After that run git submodule update --init --recursive.

See the docs for git submodule init and git config submodule.<name>.active.

BTW, .gitmodules doesn't have attribute active.
